The lunatic, the lover, and the poet, / Are of imagination all compact.
column2: Theseus says this in 5.1.8-10, grouping those three as people whose "shaping fantasies" outrun "cool reason."

column1: gives to airy nothing / A local habitation and a name
column2: Theseus says this of the poet's pen in 5.1.17-19, describing how imagination turns unknown forms into shapes, places, and people.

column1: How easy is a bush suppos'd a bear!
column2: Theseus says this in 5.1.23-24 as an everyday example of how "strong imagination" can turn a night-time fear into a supposed beast.

column1: grows to something of great constancy
column2: Hippolyta says this in 5.1.25-28, arguing that the lovers' shared, consistent story of the night "more witnesseth than fancy's images."

column1: A tedious brief scene of young Pyramus / And his love Thisbe; very tragical mirth.
column2: Theseus reads this from Philostrate's paper in 5.1.61-63, then wonders at the oxymorons "merry and tragical" and "tedious and brief."

column1: never anything can be amiss, / When simpleness and duty tender it.
column2: Theseus says this in 5.1.88-90 when he overrules Philostrate and agrees to hear the hard-handed men's play.

column1: This fellow doth not stand upon points.
column2: Theseus says this in 5.1.128 after Quince's prologue, meaning the speaker misuses punctuation and pauses in the wrong places.

column1: The best in this kind are but shadows, and the worst are no worse, if imagination amend them.
column2: Theseus tells Hippolyta this in 5.1.209-210 after she calls the play "the silliest stuff that ever I heard."

column1: I, one Snug the joiner, am / A lion-fell, nor else no lion's dam.
column2: Snug, playing Lion, says this in 5.1.218-219 so the ladies will not fear he is a real lion.

column1: This is old Ninny's tomb. Where is my love?
column2: Thisbe (Flute) says this in 5.1.240, repeating the mechanicals' habitual mix-up of Ninus with "Ninny."

column1: Now die, die, die, die, die.
column2: Bottom, as Pyramus, says this in 5.1.282 as he stabs himself, after which Demetrius puns that he is "no die, but an ace."

column1: let your epilogue alone
column2: Theseus says this in 5.1.320-323 after refusing Bottom's offered epilogue and asking instead for a Bergomask dance.

column1: 'tis almost fairy time.
column2: Theseus says this in 5.1.323 when midnight has "told twelve," sending the lovers to bed and opening the way for the fairies' blessing.

column1: If we shadows have offended, / Think but this, and all is mended, / That you have but slumber'd here.
column2: Puck says this in 5.2.56-59, asking the audience to take the play as a dream and, if they are friends, to give him their hands.
